"Hello, Dolly!" is the title song of the popular musical of the same name, with music and lyrics by Jerry Herman.

A recording by Louis Armstrong released in 1964 was a widely popular success, winning the Song of the Year and Male Vocal Performance awards at the 7th Annual Grammy Awards. Armstrong's rendition was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2001.

sections.heading: History
sections.wikitext:
At the behest of his manager, [[Louis Armstrong]] made a demonstration recording of "Hello, Dolly!" in December 1963, for the song's publisher to use to promote the [[Broadway (theatre)|Broadway]] show.<ref>[{{Allmusic|class=song|id=t4280502|pure_url=yes}} All Music: Hello, Dolly! history]</ref> 

In January 1964, the same month ''Hello, Dolly!'' opened in New York City, [[Kapp Records]] released Armstrong's publishing demo as a commercial single. His version reached {{abbr|No.|number}} 1 on the U.S. [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], ending [[the Beatles]]' streak of [[List_of_Billboard_Hot_100_number_ones_of_1964|3 chart-topping hits in a row over 14 consecutive weeks]]. 

"Hello Dolly!" became the most successful single of Armstrong's career, followed by a Gold-selling album of the same name.<ref>Bronson, Fred. ''The Billboard Book of Number 1 Hits'' (2003), Billboard Books, {{ISBN|0-8230-7677-6}}</ref> The song also spent nine weeks atop the [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|adult contemporary chart]] shortly after the opening of the musical. The song also made Armstrong the oldest artist ever to reach {{abbr|No.|number}} 1 on the Hot 100 since its introduction in 1958. ''Billboard'' ranked the record as the {{abbr|No.|number}} 3 song of 1964, behind the Beatles' "[[I Want to Hold Your Hand]]" and "[[She Loves You]]".<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1964]]</ref>

"Hello, Dolly!" won the [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year]] in 1965, and Armstrong received a Grammy for [[Grammy Award for Best Vocal Performance, Male|Best Vocal Performance, Male]]. Louis Armstrong also performed the song alongside [[Barbra Streisand]] for the [[Hello, Dolly! (film)|musical's 1969 screen adaptation]]. In 2018, the song was listed at number 178 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 60th Anniversary chart.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100-60th-anniversary|title=Billboard Hot 100 60th Anniversary Interactive Chart|magazine=Billboard|access-date=10 December 2018}}</ref> There were other charting versions of the song also in 1964 by Kenny Ball, Frankie Vaughan, The Batchelors and Frank Sinatra. Liberace also recorded a vocal version of the song.
sections.text:
At the behest of his manager, Louis Armstrong made a demonstration recording of "Hello, Dolly!" in December 1963, for the song's publisher to use to promote the Broadway show. 

In January 1964, the same month Hello, Dolly! opened in New York City, Kapp Records released Armstrong's publishing demo as a commercial single. His version reached {{abbr|No.|number}} 1 on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100, ending the Beatles' streak of 3 chart-topping hits in a row over 14 consecutive weeks. 

"Hello Dolly!" became the most successful single of Armstrong's career, followed by a Gold-selling album of the same name. The song also spent nine weeks atop the adult contemporary chart shortly after the opening of the musical. The song also made Armstrong the oldest artist ever to reach {{abbr|No.|number}} 1 on the Hot 100 since its introduction in 1958. Billboard ranked the record as the {{abbr|No.|number}} 3 song of 1964, behind the Beatles' "I Want to Hold Your Hand" and "She Loves You".

"Hello, Dolly!" won the Grammy Award for Song of the Year in 1965, and Armstrong received a Grammy for Best Vocal Performance, Male. Louis Armstrong also performed the song alongside Barbra Streisand for the musical's 1969 screen adaptation. In 2018, the song was listed at number 178 on the Billboard Hot 100 60th Anniversary chart. There were other charting versions of the song also in 1964 by Kenny Ball, Frankie Vaughan, The Batchelors and Frank Sinatra. Liberace also recorded a vocal version of the song.

sections.heading: "Hello, Lyndon!"
sections.wikitext: [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] used the tune, rechristened "Hello, Lyndon!", as a [[campaign song]] for his run in the [[1964 United States presidential election|1964 U.S. presidential election]]. This version of the song was performed by [[Carol Channing]] at that year's [[1964 Democratic National Convention|Democratic National Convention]], and a recording was made by [[Ed Ames]] for distribution at the convention.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/08/21/archives/hello-lyndon-joins-campaign-at-democratic-parley-next-week-herman.html|title='Hello, Lyndon!' Joins Campaign At Democratic Parley Next Week; Herman, Composer, to Play Song for Carol Channing at Atlantic City Meeting|newspaper=The New York Times|page=15|date=August 21, 1964|access-date=August 26, 2018}}</ref>

sections.heading: The "Sunflower" controversy
sections.wikitext: "Hello, Dolly!" became caught up in a lawsuit which could have endangered plans for filming the musical. [[Mack David]], a composer, sued for infringement of copyright, because the first four [[bar (music)|bar]]s of "Hello, Dolly!"  were the same as those in the [[refrain]] of David's song "Sunflower" from 1948. As he recounts in his memoirs, Herman had never heard "Sunflower" before the lawsuit, and wanted a chance to defend himself in court, but, for the sake of those involved in the show and the potential film, he reluctantly agreed to pay a settlement before the case would have gone to trial.<ref> Riedel, Michael. [http://www.nydailynews.com/play-jerry-broadway-tunesmith-jerry-herman-back-years-revue-article-1.815870 "Play it Again, Jerry. Broadway Tunesmith Jerry herman Looks Back on Years in Revue".] ''New York Daily News''.  12 July 1998.</ref><ref>Herman, Jerry (with Marilyn Stasio). ''Showtune: A Memoir''. New York: Donald I. Fine Books, 1996, pp. 102–108.</ref>
sections.text: "Hello, Dolly!" became caught up in a lawsuit which could have endangered plans for filming the musical. Mack David, a composer, sued for infringement of copyright, because the first four bars of "Hello, Dolly!"  were the same as those in the refrain of David's song "Sunflower" from 1948. As he recounts in his memoirs, Herman had never heard "Sunflower" before the lawsuit, and wanted a chance to defend himself in court, but, for the sake of those involved in the show and the potential film, he reluctantly agreed to pay a settlement before the case would have gone to trial.

sections.heading: In popular culture
sections.wikitext: *In 1984, Carol Channing sang a parody of the song on ''[[Sesame Street]]'' called "Hello, Sammy!", a love song to a [[List of Sesame Street Muppets|character]] known as Sammy the Snake (as voiced by its creator, [[Jim Henson]]). Carol tells Sammy just how much she loves and adores him while Sammy coils himself around Carol's arms. They are soon joined by four giant, swaying letter [[S]]'s wearing a [[top hat]]s. Carol ends the song by telling Sammy how much she'd miss his hisses if they ever parted.<ref>{{YouTube|CNyr1CzTSeU|”Carol Channing sings “Hello, Sammy!” to Sammy the Snake”}}</ref>
